meta.blurb: Twelve-year-old Kofi is brilliant at a tide game, so the Tide Academy invites him to train on its great Simulation. He works, learns and wins every test. Then comes the final exam, and nothing about it is what he believes.
meta.bible: Kofi Asante: twelve, from a seaweed-farming family in the delta near Port Halden; clever, stubborn, kind. Abena: his sister, eight, draws. Efua Asante: his mother. Gran: his grandmother, proud and sharp. Commander Ruth Halloran: head of the Tide Academy, stern, honest in the end. Dr Pavel Lind: Kofi's gentle instructor. Mei-Lin Tran: thirteen, careful planner, Kofi's friend. Joaquin Ferro: fourteen, big laugh, Kofi's friend. Samira Qadir: thirteen, top of the class, fast and proud, becomes a friend. Port Halden: the big city on the delta, protected by sea walls. Highfield Station: the Academy, high in the hills inland. Tide Academy: the school that trains young pilots. The Simulation, also called the Game: the tank-room map where pilots command drones. Floats: small floating rescue drones that carry sandbags, close gates and lift people. Delta Command: the advanced class. The Last Tide: the final exam, which is really the real storm. East Bend: a weak part of the sea wall. Mill Fields: the low farmland outside the city. Hill School: where the evacuated families wait. The tide puzzle: the tablet game Kofi plays at home. Voice: warm close third person, past tense, tense and hopeful; no gore; no real people. Pilots are twelve to fourteen; the storm is a real surge in the near future.

B1B2: Kofi Asante lives on a seaweed farm in the delta, and every morning he plays the tide puzzle on a cracked tablet. Today he sets a new record, which no one in the world has beaten.

That evening a letter with a bright blue seal arrives from the Tide Academy, and the family gathers around the kitchen table. It says that Kofi has been chosen to train on the Simulation, and Mum is worried while Abena asks if he will come back.
The news shows the sea walls of Port Halden, and the sea beyond them is higher and angrier than last year. Mum says that storms are getting bigger, and Abena draws a boat beside her brother's name.

Commander Ruth Halloran arrives the next morning, tall and serious in a dark blue coat. She explains that the Academy trains young people to command small rescue drones called floats, but she never says what the floats are really for.

Kofi hugs his mother and grandmother on the platform, and Abena gives him a drawing of a boat to keep. The train pulls away past the great sea wall, and he watches the sea shrink to a thin silver line.
Highfield Station sits among cold hills, a long grey building with bright windows and a view of nothing but fog. A big boy with a loud laugh takes Kofi's bag and says that his name is Joaquin.
In the dining hall Kofi meets Mei-Lin Tran, who writes everything in a tiny notebook, and Samira Qadir. Samira's name is at the top of a ranking board, and Kofi's own name is at the very bottom.

In the great tank-room, Dr Pavel Lind switches on the Simulation, and a glowing map of a river delta spreads across the table. Hundreds of small floats sit on it like beads, and each pilot can command them with a touch or a spoken word.
His first exercise is simple, but Kofi panics and closes the wrong gate, and the blue flood spreads over the whole map. The other pilots finish in minutes, and he is sure that he will be sent home.

Dr Lind finds him afterwards, sitting alone beside the map, and tells him not to be ashamed. Most pilots stare at the water, he says, but the best ones ask where it wants to go and then make that path easy.

That night, while the others sleep, Kofi creeps back to the tank-room and practises until his eyes burn. He learns that each float has only a few hours of power, and that floats in a chain pass sandbags faster.

Samira is faster than anyone, and her floats move across the map in neat, perfect rows. But when the exercise changes without warning, her rows break, and she tells Kofi afterwards that real pilots do not guess.

In the first team exercise, Kofi is given ten floats and told to build a wall of sandbags against a rising tide. Instead of using straight lines, he makes the floats move like starlings, and his wall stands while three others fall.

After a few weeks, Kofi writes a long letter home about the floats, the hills and Joaquin's snoring. Mum writes back that the storms are growing worse, and she sends a drawing from Abena of a boy flying a kite over the waves.

The Commander makes the tests harder and harder, and sometimes the Simulation seems to change its rules in the middle of a task. Kofi begins to wonder whether the Game cheats, but Dr Lind only says that real storms never keep to a timetable.

One cold night Kofi lies awake missing the smell of the sea, and Joaquin climbs down from his bunk with two mugs of tea. He tells ridiculous stories about his old school until Kofi laughs so hard that his sides hurt.
On a hard exercise, Kofi tries something new and opens a gate to let the flood spill across the low fields. The town stays dry, but the Simulation counts the fields as lost, so his score is poor.

Commander Halloran dislikes the idea because it means giving up the farmland, and she tells him sharply that the score counts crops. But the town was saved, so she cannot argue, and Samira's name stays above his.

One morning, the Commander calls out four names in a row: Kofi, Mei-Lin, Samira and Joaquin. They have been chosen for the advanced class, called Delta Command, and from tomorrow they will train in a different room with a bigger map.
The new room is round and dark, with four glowing consoles and a huge map that curls around the walls. Kofi is given the middle district, the sea gate itself, and he feels both proud and frightened.

In the first big exercise, Kofi's district floods, and he demands that Samira send him floats, but she refuses. Mei-Lin asks them quietly what they are both afraid of, and after a long pause Samira sends half her floats.

Mei-Lin shows Kofi how to read the pressure lines and wind arrows in the weather charts that feed the Simulation. The storms in the Game, Kofi notices, are not invented ones, because they behave like real weather.

One evening Kofi looks closely at the district map and sees a bridge, a market and a street he knows well. When he asks about it, Commander Halloran says briskly that they train on the places they are going to protect.

The students are forbidden to watch the news or use their phones, because the Commander says it would break their concentration. Mum's last letter has not come, and a teacher says that the post is slow in bad weather, but Kofi does not believe it.

Joaquin creeps to a window and points out at the hills, where a heavy dark sky is gathering and the rain comes sideways. The instructors hurry through the corridors with grey faces, and Kofi feels that something is happening that nobody will explain.

Late that night, Dr Lind stops Kofi in the corridor and presses a small carved whistle into his hand. Whatever happens, he says, you are better at this than you know, and the words sound to Kofi like a goodbye.

The next morning, the Commander tells the four of them that the final exam, the Last Tide, will begin the following day. It will last from morning until night, she says, and nothing in the Academy can prepare them for it.

The four of them eat together that night in the empty hall, and nobody wants to speak of tomorrow. Samira tells Kofi that she is sorry for calling him lucky, and Mei-Lin passes round a smooth grey stone.

At dawn the four pilots take their places in the round room, and the map glows softly around them. Commander Halloran tells them to treat everything as real and to remember that every light on the map is a life.

In the first hour the map shows only a slow, grey swell far out at sea, and a ring of low pressure is gathering strength. Kofi sends floats to check the gates, and nothing seems to be wrong yet, but he knows that a storm can grow fast.

By the third hour, the wind has risen sharply, and the sea begins to climb against the walls of the delta. Kofi spreads his floats along the sea gate in a long, thin line, ready to reinforce any weak point.

The surge arrives in the fifth hour, a mountain of water pushing against the sea gate, and one of the great doors jams halfway open. Kofi sends forty floats to drag a cable around the gate and heap sandbags against it, and slowly the door holds.

In the sixth hour, the East Bend wall cracks in Samira's district, and water pours through the gap. Kofi does not hesitate but sends half of his own floats across the map, and together they plug the crack.

By the seventh hour the sea is too strong for the wall, so Kofi remembers his old idea about the fields. He sends boats to Mill Fields to collect every family, and only then does he let the sea spill across the land.

Behind the glass wall of the tank-room, the instructors watch in complete silence, and some of them have their hands over their mouths. Dr Lind whispers something to the Commander, and she grips the radio so tightly that her knuckles turn white.

The surge peaks in the eighth hour, and the whole sea seems to lean against the delta. Kofi holds the line with six hundred floats, and he rotates them through the charging bays so that none goes dark.

In the ninth hour, water begins to creep into the hospital district, and Mei-Lin cries out that she has no floats left. Kofi sends her every spare machine he has, and she lifts a wall of sandbags just in time.

In the tenth hour, the winds soften, the surge slides back, and the red lights on the map turn slowly to green. The four pilots shout and hug one another, but when Kofi looks up at the glass, the instructors are not cheering.

The door of the tank-room opens, and a crowd of adults pours in, many with tears on their faces. Commander Halloran kneels and takes Kofi's hands, and she tells him in a cracked voice that it was never a test.
Dr Lind turns on a screen, and Kofi sees a live view of Port Halden under heavy clouds. Small floats, the same ones he commanded, are carrying people through the muddy streets to safety.
Kofi steps back and tells Commander Halloran that she lied to them, and his voice shakes with anger. She says that fear would have made them slower, so she hid the truth, and she is truly sorry.

Kofi turns to Dr Lind and asks, in a very small voice, whether his own family was in the city. Dr Lind scrolls through a long list of evacuated families and finds Efua Asante, Gran and Abena, who are safe at the Hill School.
Kofi shakes with sobs, and Samira, Mei-Lin and Joaquin put their arms around him until the four of them are a single knot. Joaquin is laughing and crying together, and nobody speaks for a long time.

The next morning, the news is finally allowed into the Academy, and the headline says that Port Halden has survived the surge. The sea walls held, the flooded farmland was empty because of the early evacuation, and more than a million people are safe.

Two days later a woman from the Port Halden hospital arrives with a cake that she has baked herself. She tells Kofi that the hospital lights never went out, and that her newborn daughter slept safely through the whole night.
Kofi asks to speak to the Commander alone, and he stands in her office with his hands clenched. He says that pilots must be told the truth in future, and Halloran bows her head and agrees.

The Board of the Academy meets in a long hall, and the four friends stand up one by one to speak. They will serve again if pilots are told when a storm is real, and after long argument the Board agrees.

When the Academy lets him go home at last, Kofi rides the train down the valley with the carved whistle in his pocket. The fields are grey with mud, but the great sea wall stands tall at the end of the valley.

The seaweed raft has survived, its ropes frayed but unbroken, and his family stands on it waiting for him. Abena runs at him so hard that she nearly knocks him into the water, and that night he tells them everything about the floats.

At dawn Kofi sits on the raft with the cracked tablet on his knees, and Abena leans against his shoulder to watch. The tide puzzle looks different now, because he knows that behind every small blue gate lies a real city, but the sea is calm.
C1C2: At dawn, on the family's seaweed raft, Kofi Asante bent over a cracked tablet and moved small blue gates to stop an imaginary flood. The tide puzzle was his favourite thing in the world, and this morning he finished it faster than anyone had before. He did not yet know that someone far away was watching the score climb past every other name on the list.

That evening a letter with a bright blue seal arrives from the Tide Academy, and the whole family gathers around the kitchen table. It says that Kofi has been chosen to train on the Simulation, and that his family must decide quickly. Gran is proud, Mum is worried, and his little sister Abena asks if he will come back.

That night the news shows the sea walls of Port Halden, and the sea beyond them is higher and angrier than last year. Mum says that storms are getting bigger and that the Academy is the best chance Kofi has to learn something useful. Abena draws a boat beside her brother's name, and Gran tells him he can always come home.

Commander Ruth Halloran arrives the next morning, tall and serious in a dark blue coat. She explains that the Academy trains young people to command fleets of small rescue drones, called floats, and that learners often adapt to new ideas faster than adults. Mum asks hard questions, and the Commander answers them honestly, except that she never says what the floats are really for.

Kofi hugged his mother and grandmother on the platform, and Abena gave him a drawing of a boat to keep in his pocket. The train pulled away from the delta, past the great sea wall and up the river valley into the hills. He pressed his face to the window until the sea had shrunk to a thin silver line and then disappeared.

Highfield Station sat among cold hills, a long grey building with bright windows and a view of nothing but fog. A big boy with a loud laugh took Kofi's bag and introduced himself as Joaquin Ferro, the fourteen-year-old who had the bunk above his. He promised that the food was bad but the pillows were good, and that was how Kofi's life at the Academy began.

In the dining hall, he met Mei-Lin Tran, a thoughtful girl who wrote everything in a tiny notebook, and Samira Qadir, whose name stood at the top of a ranking board on the wall. Samira looked at him as if he were a small, odd fish, and Mei-Lin whispered that she was very good and knew it. Kofi looked at the board and saw that his own name was at the very bottom.

In the great tank-room, Dr Pavel Lind switched on the Simulation, and a glowing map of a river delta spread across the table. Hundreds of small floats sat on it like beads, and each pilot could command them with a touch or a spoken word. Kofi stared, because the map looked strangely alive, as if real water was moving somewhere under the glass.

His first exercise was simple, but Kofi panicked and closed the wrong gate, and the blue flood spread over the whole map. The other pilots finished in minutes while he was still sending his floats in circles. When the red lights stopped blinking, he felt hot with embarrassment, and he was sure he would be sent home.

Dr Lind found him afterwards, sitting alone beside the map, and told him not to be ashamed. He said that most pilots stared at the water, but the best ones asked where it wanted to go and then made that path easy. Kofi thought about the tide puzzle at home, and for the first time all day he felt a little braver.

That night, while the others slept, Kofi crept back to the tank-room and practised until his eyes burned. He learned that each float had only a few hours of power, that a chain of floats could pass sandbags faster than a single one could carry them, and that a gate cost more time to close than it seemed. The map was no longer a puzzle to him but something he began to understand.

Samira was faster than anyone, and her floats moved across the map in neat, perfect rows. But when the exercise changed without warning, her neat rows broke, and Kofi saw her bite her lip. She told him afterwards that he had been lucky and that real pilots did not guess, and he decided not to argue.

In the first team exercise, Kofi was given ten floats and told to build a wall of sandbags against a rising tide. Instead of sending the floats in straight lines, he made them move like starlings, in a flowing shape that bent around every new problem. Dr Lind watched with his arms folded, and when the exercise ended, Kofi's wall stood while three others had fallen.

After a few weeks, Kofi wrote a long letter home about the floats and the hills and Joaquin's snoring. Mum wrote back that the storms were growing worse and that the sea walls were being checked every day, and she sent a drawing from Abena of a boy flying a kite over the waves. He pinned it above his bunk and read it every night before he slept.

The Commander made the tests harder and harder, and sometimes the Simulation seemed to change its rules in the middle of a task. A gate that should have worked would jam, or a storm would arrive an hour before it was due. Kofi began to wonder whether the Game cheated, but when he asked, Dr Lind only smiled thinly and said that real storms never kept to a timetable either.

One cold night Kofi lay awake missing the smell of the sea, and Joaquin climbed down from his bunk with two mugs of tea. He told ridiculous stories about his old school until Kofi laughed so hard that his sides hurt. Kofi realised that he had found a friend, and that he no longer felt quite so far from home.

On a particularly hard exercise, Kofi tried something nobody had taught him, and he opened a gate to let the flood spill across the low fields beside the city. The water spread out thin and harmless there, and the town stayed dry behind it. The Simulation counted the fields as lost, so his score was poor, but Dr Lind quietly told him that this was the cleverest thing he had seen all year.

Commander Halloran disliked the idea at first, because it meant giving up the farmland, and she told him sharply that the score counted crops as well as people. But the town had been saved, and she could not argue with that, so she let the matter rest. Samira's name stayed above his on the wall, but several other students were beginning to watch what Kofi did.

One morning, the Commander called out four names in a row: Kofi, Mei-Lin, Samira and Joaquin. They had been chosen for the advanced class, called Delta Command, and from tomorrow they would train in a different room with a bigger map. Kofi grinned at Joaquin, and Samira pretended not to care, though her fingers tightened on her notebook.

The new room was round and dark, with four glowing consoles and a huge map that curled around the walls like the inside of a shell. Each student took charge of one district of the delta, and Kofi was given the middle, the sea gate itself. It was the busiest and most important place, and he felt both proud and frightened.

In the first big exercise, Kofi's district was flooded and he asked Samira to send floats, but she refused. They shouted at each other until Mei-Lin stepped between them and asked quietly what they were both afraid of. Kofi admitted that he had been demanding help instead of asking, and Samira, after a long pause, sent half her floats.

Mei-Lin showed Kofi how to read the pressure lines and wind arrows in the weather charts that fed the Simulation. She explained that low pressure draws the sea upward and that wind pushes it toward land, and that together they can make a surge. The storms in the Game, Kofi noticed, were not at all like invented ones, because they behaved with all the small, untidy habits of real weather.

One evening, Kofi looked closely at the district map and saw a bridge, a market and a street he knew well. It was the delta around Port Halden, and one small square was the road where his seaweed raft was moored. When he asked about it, Commander Halloran said briskly that they trained on the places they were going to protect, and the answer sounded perfectly reasonable.

The students were forbidden to watch the news or use their phones, because the Commander said it would break their concentration. Mum's last letter had not come, and when Kofi asked about it, a teacher said that the post was slow in bad weather. He did not believe it, but he was too tired to push, and the uneasy feeling settled into his stomach like a stone.

Joaquin crept to a window and pointed out at the hills, where a heavy dark sky was gathering and the rain came sideways. The instructors hurried through the corridors with grey faces, and one of them snapped at a student for no reason at all. Kofi felt that something was happening beyond the walls of Highfield Station, something that nobody would explain.

Late that night, Dr Lind stopped Kofi in the corridor and pressed a small carved whistle into his hand. It had belonged to his own father, he said, who had been a sailor, and it was meant to bring good luck. Whatever happens, he told Kofi, you are better at this than you know, and the words sounded to Kofi like a goodbye.

The next morning, the Commander stood before the four of them and announced that the final exam, the Last Tide, would begin the following day. It would last from morning until night and would test everything they had learned, she said, and nothing in the Academy could prepare them for it. Her voice was perfectly steady, but Kofi noticed the shadows beneath her eyes and understood that she had not slept in many nights.

The four of them ate together that night in the empty hall, and nobody wanted to speak of tomorrow. Samira turned to Kofi and said she was sorry for calling him lucky, because he was the best pilot she had ever seen. Mei-Lin passed round a smooth grey stone she said had brought her luck all year, and each of them held it for a moment.

At dawn the four pilots took their places in the round room, and the map glowed softly around them. Commander Halloran told them to treat everything as real, to trust their training and to remember that every light on the map was a life. Then she stepped back, and the Last Tide began, and the tank-room fell silent.

In the first hour, the map showed only a slow, grey swell far out at sea, and a ring of low pressure was gathering strength. Kofi sent floats to check the gates and test the walls, and nothing seemed to be wrong yet. But he remembered Mei-Lin's lessons, and he knew that a storm like this could grow far faster than anyone expected.

By the third hour, the wind had risen sharply, and the sea began to climb against the walls of the delta. Kofi spread his floats along the sea gate in a long, thin line, ready to reinforce any weak point. Beside him Samira worked in silence, and Joaquin muttered encouragement to his floats as if they were a herd of nervous sheep.

The surge arrived in the fifth hour, a mountain of water pushing against the sea gate, and one of the great doors jammed halfway open. Kofi did not panic this time, but sent forty floats to drag a cable around the gate and heap sandbags against it. The door shuddered, held and slowly stopped letting water through, and he let out a breath he had not known he was holding.

In the sixth hour, the East Bend wall fractured in Samira's district, and the sea came pouring through the breach. Samira's voice was tight with fear, but Kofi did not hesitate for a moment, and he dispatched half of his own floats across the map to reinforce her. Together they plugged the crack, and Samira whispered a hasty thank you without once turning her head from the glowing screen.

By the seventh hour, the sea had grown too strong to hold back at the wall, and Kofi remembered his old idea about the fields. He sent boats to Mill Fields to collect every family from the farms, and only then did he open a slow channel to let the sea spill across the farmland. It was a terrible choice, but the water spread out thinly there, and the city behind it began to breathe again.

Behind the glass wall of the tank-room, the instructors watched in complete silence, and some of them had their hands over their mouths. Dr Lind whispered something to the Commander, and she gripped the radio so tightly that her knuckles went white. Kofi glanced up once and wondered why a mere exam could frighten grown people so much.

The surge peaked in the eighth hour, and the whole sea seemed to lean against the delta. Kofi held the line with six hundred floats, rotating them in and out of the charging bays so that none went dark at the wrong moment. His hands were shaking, but his thoughts were clear and calm, as they had been on the family's raft long ago.

In the ninth hour, water began to creep into the hospital district, and Mei-Lin cried out that she had no floats left. Kofi sent her every spare machine he had, even the ones that were nearly out of power, and she lifted a wall of sandbags just in time. The lights of the hospital stayed on, and Mei-Lin laughed and cried at the same time.

In the tenth hour, the winds softened, the great surge slid back into the sea, and the red lights on the map turned slowly to a calm green. The four of them shouted and embraced one another, and Joaquin lifted Kofi clean off the floor in his delight. But when Kofi glanced up at the glass, he saw that the instructors were not cheering, and the silence in the room was strange and heavy.

The door of the tank-room swung open, and a crowd of adults poured in, many of them with tears streaming down their faces. They began to applaud, and Commander Halloran knelt in front of Kofi and took both of his hands in hers. It was not an examination, she told him in a voice that cracked, and it had never been one.

Dr Lind turned on a screen, and Kofi saw a live view of Port Halden under heavy clouds, with the real sea wall holding against the real waves. Small floats, the same ones he had commanded, were moving through muddy streets and carrying people to safety. He recognised the market, the bridge and the clock tower, and his legs went weak beneath him.

Kofi stepped back and told Commander Halloran that she had lied to them, and his voice shook with anger. She said that if the pilots had known that real people were at stake, fear would have made them slower and less clever, and so she had chosen to hide the truth. She would probably choose it again, she admitted, but she was truly sorry for the pain it caused.

Kofi turned to Dr Lind and asked, in a very small voice, whether his own family had been in the city. Dr Lind said gently that they had, and then scrolled through a long list of evacuated families until he found a name. Efua Asante, Gran and Abena had all been taken to the Hill School and were safe, and the tears came all at once.

Kofi shook with sobs, and Samira, Mei-Lin and Joaquin put their arms around him until the four of them were a single knot. Joaquin was laughing and crying together, and Mei-Lin passed him her lucky stone without a word. Nobody spoke for a long time, and that silence said everything that needed saying.

The next morning, the news was finally allowed into the Academy, and the headline said that Port Halden had survived the surge. The sea walls had held, the flooded farmland had been empty because of the early evacuation, and more than a million people were safe. Kofi read it twice, and the numbers meant nothing until he thought of every window in Port Halden and every one of the lights in them.

Two days later, a woman from the Port Halden hospital arrived at the Academy with a cake that she had baked herself. She held Kofi's hand and told him that the hospital lights had never gone out, and that her own newborn daughter had slept safely through the whole night. Kofi did not know what to say, so he said thank you, and she laughed and said that it should be her saying that.

Kofi asked to speak to the Commander alone, and he stood in her office with his hands clenched. He said that the pilots must be told the truth in future, because trusting them was the only way to deserve their best. Halloran listened with her head bowed, and then she agreed that he was right and promised to take the matter to the Board.

The Board of the Academy convened in a long, solemn hall, and the four friends rose one by one to address it. They declared that they were proud of what they had accomplished and willing to serve again, but only if future pilots were told when a storm was real. The Board debated for hours, and at last it voted to change its rules, so that honesty would be owed to every pilot.

When the Academy let him go home at last, Kofi rode the train down the valley with the carved whistle in his pocket. The fields were grey with mud, and the river was high, but the great sea wall stood tall at the end of the valley. He pressed his face to the window, and the sea came back to him, brown and tired and beautiful.

The seaweed raft had survived, its ropes frayed but unbroken, and his family stood on it waiting for him. Abena ran at him so hard that she nearly knocked him into the water, and Mum and Gran held on to him as if he might float away. That night he told them about the floats and the Simulation, and Gran said she had always known he would do something great.

At dawn, Kofi sat on the raft with the cracked tablet on his knees, and Abena leaned against his shoulder to watch. The tide puzzle looked different now, because he knew that behind every small blue gate lay a real city full of real lights. He moved a gate gently, the sea lay calm all round them, and for once he was glad that the game was only a game.
